item.title: China’s Sports Reform Must Give Ordinary Children Somewhere to Play
item.description:
When a team accustomed to winning starts losing repeatedly, the first thing to falter is often not a particular technique but the audience’s confidence that someone will always step up. In the summer of 2026, China’s men’s singles table-tennis players suffered successive defeats while Fan Zhendong competed for a German club. Put the two images together and an easy explanation emerges: the strongest player has gone abroad, and those left behind cannot take over.

The question deserves a serious answer. But judging what has gone wrong in player development requires connecting results, athletes’ movement and the paths available to ordinary children. A medals table cannot speak for every part of the system.

Repeated defeats are a real problem; their causes need separating

By the Macau event on September 12, Chinese men had failed to reach the singles semifinals at four consecutive major WTT events: the US Smash, Yokohama Champions, Sweden Smash and Macau Champions. In the United States they stopped a round earlier. Wang Chuqin lost 1–3 to Anders Lind in the round of 16, and Lin Shidong lost 0–3 to Alexis Lebrun, leaving China without a men’s singles quarterfinalist. US results, summary of the four events

Macau had different conditions. Wang Chuqin and Lin Shidong were absent through injury. Huang Youzheng lost to Kanak Jha in the first round, Chen Yuanyu lost to Darko Jorgić in the round of 16, and Zhou Qihao lost 1–4 to Tomokazu Harimoto in the quarterfinals. Injuries and the lineup explain part of the background to that event; they cannot retrospectively explain the US defeats when the leading players were present.

Four events provide sufficient grounds to review squad depth, training and changes among opponents. They also show that the old expectation of reliably sweeping the honors is no longer dependable. But the results alone do not prove unfair selection, nor that Fan’s move abroad caused the defeats. Chinese women’s singles and doubles still produced strong results. Sun Yingsha and Kuai Man met in the US women’s singles final. Pressure on the men’s singles team should not become a claim that all Chinese table tennis has lost competitiveness.

Fan’s position also needs accurate description. He withdrew from the world rankings at the end of 2024; that was not an announcement of retirement. In July 2026 he moved from Saarbrücken to Düsseldorf for the 2026/27 season. A club match report on August 23 recorded two singles wins. Club report

Whether established athletes may play abroad and how the national team evaluates and uses them are two sets of rules that need to connect. Treating movement as an automatic loss of talent overlooks overseas leagues as opportunities to train and compete. Conversely, if the assessment system cannot explain how overseas results enter selection decisions, questions from athletes and spectators will not disappear on their own.

How far have Japan’s and Germany’s young players progressed?

Japan’s Sora Matsushima defeated Harimoto in the semifinals of the 2026 All Japan Championships and Hiroto Shinozuka 4–0 in the final, winning the title for a second successive year. He later beat Vladimir Sidorenko 4–2 in the US Smash final. Shinozuka also defeated Wen Ruibo and Hugo Calderano at that event. These are signs of young players delivering in high-level senior competition, not merely promising names on a junior-team roster. Japan Table Tennis Association, full US results

Germany’s evidence is at another level. Two Germans, Andre Bertelsmeier and Wim Verdonschot, met in the men’s singles final of the 2026 European Under-21 Championships, with Bertelsmeier winning 4–3. That identifies prospects worth watching. There remains a distance between an Under-21 title and the top of the senior world game. Nor can a German club employing Fan be credited as German youth development producing an Olympic champion. European Table Tennis Union report

Likewise, a stretch of defeats for young Chinese players does not mean nobody can compete. Lin Shidong has already achieved high-level international results. The issue is whether players can respond consistently to different opponents and keep challenging for leading roles, not whether there has ever been a young champion.

Testing a claim of a missing generation requires sustained observation of peers’ senior appearances, performances against strong opponents, injuries and depth. Comparing the single best young player abroad with everyone who lost at one Chinese outing turns a real problem into an emotional assertion.

What gold medals prove, and what they leave unanswered

China’s women’s volleyball team won five successive major world titles from 1981 to 1986 and another Olympic title in 2016. Those achievements reflect real training and competitive ability. Concentrated resources do not make them count for less. But a national team’s victories do not tell us whether ordinary students have courts, whether a county can sustain a league, or whether children who were not selected can continue playing.

Centralized development is good at directing limited resources toward a small number of high-potential athletes, maintaining access to coaches, medical support and intensive training. Its vulnerable point is whether those rejected early, or unsuited to highly centralized living, have another route. The earlier selection comes and the higher the cost of leaving, the more likely families are to treat one trial as a decision about a child’s entire future.

Football, basketball and volleyball depend especially on repeated competition over long periods. A place on a training-camp roster is not the same as gaining decision-making experience against opponents. Weekly matches, minutes played and the quality of opposition tell us more about development than the number of activities attended in a year. That is why adding designated schools alone may not deliver results.

More community teams and clubs do not automatically mean fairness

Having schools, communities and clubs alongside one another lets children participate first and gradually choose how much to commit. There are observers beyond one coach. Rejection by one institution may be followed by an opportunity in another league, club or age group. German football’s regional talent network offers an organizational approach different from a single centralized selection. Yet one country and one sport cannot stand for all sport abroad.

The real value of such a route lies in preserving another chance: a late developer gets more years, someone changing sports can start again, and someone whose interest never becomes a career can keep participating.

Markets have barriers of their own. Project Play’s survey of families participating in youth sports found average annual spending of $1,016 on one child’s primary sport in 2024, 46% above 2019. This is not an average across all US households, but it is enough to show that club routes can select families by money, transport and parents’ time. Survey explanation

Professional prospects are even less suitable as a promise of widespread returns. NCAA estimates for men’s basketball in 2024 counted approximately 43 NBA selections among an estimated 4,359 draft-eligible players, or about 1%. This measures the NBA draft alone, not the share reaching any professional basketball opportunity. Even within that limit, it shows why the earnings of a few successful athletes cannot underwrite an ordinary family’s training bills.

Coaches responsible only for immediate results may also favor children who mature earlier and can win now. Multiple institutions offer chances to correct such judgments, but that requires transfers, appropriate groupings and matches for those not selected. Otherwise, “free choice” may simply mean that affluent families can afford more chances.

Reform has begun; the next test is the participant’s experience and costs

The 2020 guidelines on integrating sports and education explicitly promoted cooperation among schools, sports schools and community sports organizations. The 2026 national youth-sports meeting continued to emphasize links between broad participation and higher performance. It would be wrong to say reform has not begun. Beijing’s 2025 Hundred Teams Cup attracted 1,369 teams, offering a concrete example of open registration and competition at multiple levels. National meeting, Beijing practice

The size of an event does not establish that every child can afford to participate or keep getting games. Whether reform reaches families can be assessed through results closer to their actual experience:

Barrier to address Results worth publishing consistently
Having a team does not guarantee matches Matches per season and actual playing time for ordinary participants
Children can participate in primary school but leave later Participation after entering junior and senior secondary school, and reasons for leaving
Training fees hide other barriers Total household spending on travel, equipment and events, and assistance for families in need
Rejected children have nowhere to go Ordinary leagues, transfers, changes of sport and routes back into mainstream education
Selection criteria are hard to understand Observation periods, assessment standards, opportunities for reconsideration and appeals

Sports schools’ professional coaches and accumulated expertise can support schools and grassroots organizations; they need not be rejected wholesale. Public money should also fund opportunities for the majority rather than follow only a few prizewinning teams. Elite development can maintain demanding standards while ordinary participants receive dependable facilities, organizers and another match.

Fan’s matches raise questions about how elite athletes are used. Repeated men’s singles defeats raise questions about who comes next. Those pressures can drive reform, but recovering a few gold medals should not be where the work ends.

A child should be able to find a court and a team on Saturday, then have another match next week after a loss. Years later, discovering that a professional career is out of reach should still leave room for normal schooling and games with friends. Whether that life becomes common is what determines whether sport has truly taken root in ordinary people’s days.

References

The discussion of competition results is current through September 15, 2026. Results from different age groups, events and years are not combined into an overall win rate.

Previously, people in China believed that table tennis was an invincible discipline for us—as long as we competed, we would win gold medals. Now things have changed: the key players we’ve cultivated have left, those who remain lack sufficient ability, and issues have emerged in the selection mechanism. This doesn’t even mention football, basketball, or volleyball. The former glory of the Chinese women’s volleyball team was also a product of the sports school era—mobilizing national efforts made everyone feel that the Chinese women’s volleyball team was incredibly strong. In foreign selection models, children in elementary school are free to participate in various sports, choosing what they like. During holidays, they can continue training at clubs. If coaches think they have potential, or if they’re spotted by scouts, they can advance to higher-level clubs, participate in youth professional leagues, and work their way up. item.title: Family Planning Thinned Kinship Networks, but Did Not Decide Who Built a Dynasty
item.description:
Fewer children mean a thinner kinship network, but not necessarily more dispersed wealth. A couple’s property and savings may end up concentrated in the hands of their only child. That counterintuitive possibility is the first obstacle to clear when discussing family planning and the power of families.

Family planning can change how many branches a family has. It cannot, by itself, explain who can pass down assets, advantages associated with official positions, and social connections. Drawing a direct line between China’s population policy and America’s wealthy dynasties conflates three questions: population size, property institutions and political organization.

The conditions in which birth restrictions developed

China’s population grew from approximately 540 million in 1949 to 830 million in 1970 and 960 million in 1978. Falling mortality and improving medical care and living conditions allowed more children to reach adulthood, while supplies of food, housing, education and jobs took time to expand. Controlling population growth became part of development policy. National Bureau of Statistics historical review

The policy did not begin in the form later generations came to know. The 1970s campaign promoted later marriage and childbearing, longer intervals between births, and fewer children. Family planning entered the Constitution in 1978. An open letter in 1980 went further in advocating one child per couple and asked Party members, Communist Youth League members and cadres to lead by example. Strict restrictions developed gradually. Family structures formed after the 1980s cannot explain retrospectively why a certain kind of family dynasty did not emerge in the early years of the People’s Republic.

Nor should an effect be rewritten as an original motive. Birth restrictions may reduce the horizontal reach of a clan, but the publicly stated policy goals concerned population growth and the capacity to support development. They do not establish that the policy was originally designed to prevent large clans or politically powerful families.

Other influences are hard to isolate: urbanization, expanding education, women’s employment and rising child-rearing costs also change reproductive choices. Today’s smaller families reflect several forces acting together. Every change cannot be charged to the same policy account.

Public employees faced an additional career consequence

Ordinary households also faced strong restrictions on childbearing. The Population and Family Planning Law as amended in 2015 provided for social maintenance fees and related enforcement measures. Their position cannot be reduced to exposure to publicity and persuasion. State employees could additionally face administrative sanctions, while workplace assessments, promotion and discipline connected family choices to their careers. The law at the time

Saying public employees were more strictly controlled is more precisely a statement that organizations possessed additional enforcement tools. So long as someone depended on an employer for a position and promotion, constraints beyond financial penalties remained effective. This explains why some families found it harder to get around the rules; it does not prove that the policy targeted their future family influence.

The introduction of the three-child policy in 2021, abolition of social maintenance fees, and moves to separate childbearing history from household registration, school admission and employment addressed these same constraints. That institutional shift cannot be adequately summarized as “all restrictions were lifted.” The 2021 policy decision

Fewer relatives do not necessarily mean less capital

The word “family” contains at least three different kinds of relationship.

Kind of family What sustains it What fewer births may change
Clan Multiple kinship branches, local ties and mutual assistance Fewer siblings and cousins, and a narrower horizontal network
Politically influential family Advantages from positions, organizational trust, education and connections Fewer relatives across different positions, while advantages may still be passed on in concentrated form
Wealthy dynasty Equity, property, inheritance arrangements and business organizations Fewer heirs, potentially leaving more resources to each heir

In the early years after the founding of the People’s Republic, an explanation of why private businesses struggled to maintain the continuity of American family companies must start with the ownership transformation of the 1950s. Property rights and business organizations changed. The number of children a family later had cannot explain those changes on its own. Nor can that historical argument be extended indefinitely: private businesses that developed again after reform and opening up now face their own succession, ownership and family-governance questions.

Positions and property must also be distinguished. A position is not a shareholding that can be inherited directly, but the education, information and social connections associated with it may shape the next generation’s starting point. Conversely, inheritance rights do not guarantee that wealth lasts forever. Business failure, division of family assets and taxation can all change the outcome.

An only-child family makes the asymmetry particularly visible. There may be fewer relatives to turn to horizontally, but more assets and care responsibilities to inherit vertically. One person can receive more family support while also bearing responsibility for aging parents alone. “Thinning the family” can mean concentrated resources and concentrated risks, not simply weaker family power.

The Rockefellers’ continuity is not explained by the number of relatives

John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil in 1870 and used a trust structure to consolidate operations in 1882. Its breakup in 1911 altered the company’s monopolistic structure without eliminating the original shareholders’ assets. A key condition for the continuation of family wealth was the existence of transferable institutional forms for corporate control, shares and investment returns. Rockefeller Archive Center

Professional managers and legal and financial institutions outside the family also mean that wealth need not depend on producing another founder in every generation. More children can expand a kinship network but may dilute equity and increase inheritance disputes. Fewer children may concentrate control. Both effects are possible; population size provides no one-way answer.

Charitable foundations require separate treatment. Donations can extend a family name’s public influence, but foundation assets cannot simply be treated as a private inheritance that descendants may spend at will. Economic wealth, institutional influence and personal spending power have become distinct. American estate taxes and antitrust rules likewise show that the continuity of private capital has always faced constraints rather than unlimited freedom.

Historical differences between China and the United States therefore cannot be reduced to one country restricting births and the other not doing so. More explanatory questions concern which assets may be privately owned and inherited, whether enterprises can survive across generations, and how families transfer control. Birth policy changes the number of participants in those processes without predetermining their results.

Why aging and difficulty finding work can coexist

At the end of 2025, China’s population was 1.40489 billion. There were 7.92 million births and 11.31 million deaths that year. People aged 60 and above numbered 323.38 million, or 23.0% of the population. At the same time, there were still 851.36 million people aged 16–59 and 725.04 million employed people nationwide. National Bureau of Statistics communiqué

Subtracting these figures does not produce an unemployment count. Age-based population statistics and employment statistics use different definitions, and the working-age population includes students and people outside the labor force. What the figures do show is that an aging country can still have a very large stock of people of working age today.

“Too few workers in the future” and “difficulty finding a job today” concern different times and different jobs. Additional births today will not enter the labor market for many years. Whether companies hire now depends on orders, profits and expectations. Automation can increase output without a proportionate increase in jobs. Care needs in one region do not automatically become jobs that graduates elsewhere are willing and able to take.

Employment pressure therefore cannot all be attributed to skills mismatch. Training can help people change occupations; it cannot create a hiring budget for a company without orders. Demand for elder care does not mean households or public services can afford it, or that workers will receive a living wage. Needs must become funded jobs before they can absorb labor.

This places a practical constraint on population policy. Asking young people to expand the future workforce cannot bypass their current income, housing, childcare and employment stability. Reducing the burden of raising children and improving life today should be two sides of the same task.

A small household may inherit two generations’ savings, yet struggle to absorb all the risks of aging, unemployment and child-rearing on its own. Discussion of population structure ultimately needs to address how those risks are shared, rather than merely asking how many new branches a family can produce.

References

  • National Bureau of Statistics: coordinating population strategy and balanced development
  • National Health Commission: response to recommendation No. 4776 at the fifth session of the 12th National People’s Congress
  • National Health Commission: deputy director’s Q&A on the universal two-child policy
  • Population and Family Planning Law, amended in 2015
  • Historical versions of Beijing’s Population and Family Planning Regulations
  • National People’s Congress: explanation of the draft amendment to the Population and Family Planning Law
  • CPPCC: socialist transformation of capitalist industry and commerce
  • Rockefeller Archive Center: John D. Rockefeller, 1839–1937
  • US Internal Revenue Service: Estate Tax Returns Revisited, 1916–1931
  • National Bureau of Statistics: 2025 national economic and social development communiqué

To a certain extent, did it limit the formation of large family clans during the early years of the founding of the People’s Republic? item.title: Capacity Expansion Is Underway. Why Won't Memory Get Cheaper Soon?
item.description:
Consumer electronics are already feeling the cost of more expensive memory, even as announcements of new capacity keep arriving. Put the two together, and it is tempting to think that phones, PCs, and SSDs should become cheaper once a few more factories open.

The difficulty lies in what happens after they open. New manufacturing capacity must turn into qualified products, those products must reach the consumer market, and only then might prices on store shelves change. Expansion adds manufacturing capability; consumers are waiting for usable supply of the products they need. The distance between the two deserves more attention than the size of the investment.

As of August 12, 2026, the available material supports a limited conclusion: the second half of 2026 looks more like a period of slower price increases; the second half of 2027 is one possible window for NAND supply and demand to ease gradually. There is no equally clear window for DRAM, and no promise of cheaper PCs, phones, or retail SSDs. This discussion concerns memory and storage chips, not all semiconductors.

Factories, bits, and products people can buy

“Capacity” has at least three meanings. Buildings and wafers provide the manufacturing base; process migrations can increase bit output per wafer; yields, packaging, testing, and product allocation determine the supply that can actually be sold. Figures in the news may all be rising while referring to different points in this chain.

TSMC’s annual capacity in 2025 exceeded 17 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers, and its projected 2026 capital spending was US$52 billion to US$56 billion, focused on advanced processes, specialty technologies, and advanced packaging. These are company-wide figures. They cannot be converted into additional DRAM or NAND supply. Samsung once planned, as of 2023, to expand cleanroom capacity to 7.3 times its 2021 level by 2027. That was a foundry target, not a measure of finished memory output.

Even for actual memory projects, the meaning of each milestone matters. Micron’s disclosed plans include several different stages:

Project Expected milestone What the milestone means
Singapore HBM advanced packaging 2027 Beginning to contribute meaningful supply
First Idaho DRAM fab Mid-2027 First wafer output
Singapore NAND fab Second half of 2028 Start of wafer output
Second Idaho DRAM fab Late 2028 First wafer output

Yields still have to ramp after the first wafers, and the product mix can change. This table is not a consumer supply schedule. SK hynix has announced construction of M15X and completed construction of M16, but its public fact sheet does not provide current monthly wafer figures on a basis that can be added to those of other manufacturers. I would rather leave that gap visible than assemble an artificially precise capacity ranking.

Another question is easier to miss: once production starts, who receives the increase? IDC projects 2026 supply growth of 16% for DRAM and 17% for NAND, while noting that resources are being directed first toward AI data-center products such as HBM and high-capacity DDR5. Samsung’s HBM4 mass production and Micron’s earlier push into HBM packaging fit that direction, but do not establish each manufacturer’s full allocation ratios.

Total supply can therefore grow while consumer supply remains tight. High-end memory, advanced packaging, and consumer chips are not fully interchangeable, so more investment need not reach ordinary SSDs sooner. Equally, blaming all the pressure on AI goes too far: processes, yields, construction schedules, and consumer demand matter as well.

Slower increases are still some distance from falling prices

TrendForce’s forecast for the third quarter of 2026 is a quarter-on-quarter increase of 13%–18% in conventional DRAM contract prices and 10%–15% in NAND Flash prices. Even if increases moderate, settlement prices are still rising. Consumers hearing that conditions are “easing” may not find a lower price on their next shopping trip.

Signal What it tells us What it cannot promise
Falling contract prices Whether upstream quarterly pricing has turned A simultaneous retail price cut
A narrowing supply-demand gap Whether the industry is approaching balance Ample supply of every product
Lower actual purchase prices Whether consumers are paying less That one promotion marks an industry turning point

TrendForce estimates a NAND supply shortfall of 4%–5% in 2026, with process migrations, bit growth, and weak consumer-electronics demand together easing conditions gradually in the second half of 2027. In this outlook, capacity growth and weakening demand both contribute to relief. The date cannot be attributed entirely to new fabs, nor can the NAND forecast be transferred to DRAM.

Why has weaker demand not immediately pushed prices down? At least in these forecasts, demand pressure has not yet eliminated the supply gap. IDC expects price acceleration to slow in the second half, while prices continue to rise and remain elevated; it projects a 17% increase in average PC selling prices in 2026. Its smartphone forecast is 1.09 billion shipments, down 13.9% year on year. Geopolitical conditions and transport costs also enter that forecast, so memory inflation cannot take all the blame.

Gartner estimates that combined DRAM and SSD prices will be 130% higher by the end of 2026 than in 2025, with PC and smartphone prices up 17% and 13%, and shipments down 10.4% and 8.4%, respectively. Its model differs from IDC’s. Both identify pressure, but their figures cannot be spliced together. An average device selling price is also not the price of a particular model: brands absorbing costs, changing configurations, and running channel promotions all affect the increase consumers actually experience.

Long-term agreements support expansion, but do not lock in profit

Multiyear contracts make some future demand more visible and help explain manufacturers’ willingness to invest. But prices, costs, and expenses still separate “customers are willing to buy” from “a minimum net profit over five years.”

Micron’s 16 disclosed Strategic Customer Agreements, or SCAs, generally cover 2026–2030; automotive agreements generally last three years. Fourteen signed agreements represent approximately US$100 billion in cumulative revenue over their remaining terms at minimum contractual prices. The 16 agreements together cover roughly 20% of DRAM shipments and one-third of NAND shipments over the period. Large contracts generally include price bands and take-or-pay arrangements.

That is a substantial revenue disclosure, but it covers only part of the business. Revenue outside the contracts, yields, product mix, depreciation, research and selling expenses, interest, and taxes can still change. Dividing US$100 billion by five and multiplying it by a current profit margin merely treats a margin from one point in the cycle as a contractual term.

The other three companies disclose less. SK hynix has confirmed multiyear LTAs with around ten customers; Samsung has confirmed 2026 HBM orders and discussions about subsequent multiyear supply; TSMC plans capacity around customers’ multiyear needs. Public information does not contain the complete economic terms needed to calculate a profit floor. TSMC’s logic-foundry earnings cannot stand in for profits on memory contracts either.

None of the four provides a basis for calculating guaranteed minimum net profit over five years. Long-term agreements improve visibility into some supply and revenue, but neither eliminate the cycle nor independently prove that consumer prices will keep rising for years.

Analyst forecasts describe scenarios, not minimum profits

The absence of a contractual profit floor does not justify giving an analyst consensus another name and using it instead. Consensus generally describes average estimated earnings at a particular date and under a particular accounting definition. The smallest figure in a sequence of forecast years is simply the smallest figure in that sequence—not the worst outcome the company could experience.

To compare manufacturers, one must retain at least the original currency, amount units, fiscal year-end, definition of net profit, and forecast publication date. Dynamic valuation pages update over time. Today’s figures cannot be backfilled as yesterday’s judgment, and missing years cannot be completed to create a five-year “guarantee.” Earnings forecasts are an especially poor substitute for evidence about individual consumer products: manufacturers may make money from high-end products while ordinary customers still face high costs.

There are differences of view as well. TrendForce identifies the second half of 2027 as a scenario for gradual relief in NAND; Micron’s June 2026 materials judge that tight conditions may persist beyond 2027. Their product scopes and perspectives differ, so they cannot be combined into a single countdown to cheaper memory.

Returning to the consumer’s question, waiting needs a specific object. First distinguish DRAM from NAND. Then watch whether contract prices turn from smaller increases to declines, whether the supply gap narrows, and what people actually pay for the capacity and configuration you need. These three signals may move at different times; they are not a mechanical purchasing countdown.

At the dates covered by these sources, NAND has a possible easing window, DRAM has no clear quarter for the start of declines, and retail prices have no confirmed reduction date. When the next capacity announcement arrives, the useful questions are: when will it produce qualified output, and how much of that output will reach the kind of product I need?

This article is an industry observation based on public information, not purchasing or investment advice.

No specific calculated data is required; data estimated by institutions is also acceptable.

item.title: A Typhoon-Day Trip to Nanjing, and a City Beneath the Streets
item.description:
A typhoon was affecting Shanghai over the weekend. When we left home that morning, the wind and rain had not yet made getting around impossible, so we followed our original plan and took the high-speed train to Nanjing for the day. My wife had arranged an easygoing itinerary, with no list of sights we had to finish. What I remembered most afterward, oddly enough, was entering a library, crossing a street, and a shopping mall’s restroom.

The library in Nanjing made a good first impression: I could walk in without swiping a card. It was a small detail, but it removed a moment of hesitation. I did not first have to work out whether I was entitled to enter. Dropping into a library while traveling also carries less pressure than visiting a sight: no hurry to take pictures or follow a route. Suddenly, the city became more than a name on a map. It was somewhere people lived their everyday lives.

The meal was less satisfying. I had been looking forward to roast duck, but what arrived was not the crispy-skinned kind I had imagined. That does not mean it was bad. Taste is hard to reason with, and my expectations had already taken a seat at the table. I still missed the roast goose in Shenzhen: a little more crispness in the skin, a more immediate richness from the fat. A local specialty cannot decide my preferences for me. Having tried it, at least I no longer had to keep imagining it.

The biggest surprise was how to get around Xinjiekou. Subway exits followed one another seemingly without end; I later found that there were at least twenty-four numbered exits. A convenient crosswalk was not always available at street level. To reach the other side, I often had to go underground and come up through another exit.

At first, this felt awkward. I could see where I wanted to go, yet could not simply walk in the most obvious direction. The underground passages connect malls and the subway, which may be convenient for people who know their way around. As a newcomer, I first had to identify the exits and work out which way to turn. Having many exits and being easy to navigate are two different things.

On a rainy day, though, the benefits became apparent. I did not have to return to the open air every time I moved somewhere else. The underground space felt like an umbrella the city had offered me. The awkward detours remained, but now I had a reason to accept them. My impression of Xinjiekou shifted between those two feelings throughout the day.

Deji Plaza is connected to this system too. It contains the familiar luxury stores; I am not their target customer, so wandering through felt rather like window shopping. What stayed with me more than the shops was the restroom people kept talking about. Some say it cost tens of millions; I cannot verify that. Still, making a restroom somewhere worth a special visit was an inventive idea.

Even someone with no intention of buying luxury goods can have a reason to enter the mall. But coming to see a restroom and choosing to shop are still a fair distance apart. I can say the mall found an entrance into people’s conversations. A single visit cannot tell me whether that improved its business.

It reminded me of Changsha IFS. Whenever I have seen its luxury floors, there have not seemed to be many people seriously browsing. Most looked as though they were passing through on their way upstairs to eat. That is only what I happened to see, of course, but it helps explain my own choices: expensive things that have no connection to my life will not keep me there. A meal I want to eat can draw me upstairs on purpose.

Looking back, the library and the mall felt approachable for different reasons. The library opened its doors without asking me to bring anything first; the mall needed to give me a reason unrelated to shopping. I like the ease of the former and can appreciate the thought behind the latter. As for Xinjiekou, what remains is not a route from a travel guide, but a very specific contrast: the other side of the street is visible above ground, yet reaching it means entering another layer of the city.
